passage: Twenty done!! Spent nine evenings going room to room with my notebook. Every conversation started the same way: "How do you get your clothes washed right now, and what does it cost you?" I was sure the answer would be "we need an app". Nobody said it. Gurleen from B block said, "I don't care about tracking. I care that it is cheaper than the shop by the gate and I know the price before I hand over the bag." Fourteen of the twenty said something like that. Surprise charges make people angry. So the thing to sort out is pricing, not screens. Good thing I had not started coding yet. Tomorrow I write the numbers into one table. — Tarun

qa.a: Fourteen of the twenty said something like that.

qa.a: Tarun feels excited and relieved: the entry begins with 'Twenty done!!' and Tarun is glad to have found out before coding.

qa.q: What alternative approach could Tarun use next, and why?
qa.a: Tarun could test a simple price list with a few volunteers, because interviews say what people want and a trial shows whether they will act on it.

qa.q: How does Gurleen see the laundry problem?
qa.a: Gurleen wants a lower price than the shop by the gate and to know the cost beforehand, so an app matters less to Gurleen than a clear price.

grounding: Shows talking to about twenty potential users before building anything and learning that pricing matters more than a technical product.

subtype: Approach: talking to twenty potential users first [Action]
passage: In the hostel of the agricultural university in Palampur, Sabina spent two evenings knocking on doors with a notepad and a packet of biscuits. Her friend Maria came along to take notes. Twenty rooms, the same questions: How do you get your clothes washed now? What do you pay? What annoys you about it? Sabina didn't mention the laundry app the two of them had sketched. By the twentieth room, the pattern was clear. Most students washed by hand or used the washerwoman from the nearby village, who charged by the bucket. What annoyed them wasn't booking. It was the cost and the time in exam weeks, when nobody could wash. "Nobody said app once," Maria said, looking at the notes. Sabina laughed, a little embarrassed. "Then the app isn't the product. A cheap exam-week wash might be."

qa.q: What did Sabina bring when knocking on doors?
qa.a: A notepad and a packet of biscuits.

qa.q: How did Sabina feel when Maria said nobody mentioned an app?
qa.a: Sabina felt a little embarrassed but amused, laughing as the planned app turned out not to matter.

qa.q: What else could Sabina test next?
qa.a: Sabina could offer a simple, cheap exam-week wash to a few rooms and see how many actually use it.

qa.q: How might the washerwoman from the village be affected by this idea?
qa.a: She could gain more exam-week work if the team works with her, or lose customers if they compete, so she has a stake in how it is done.

grounding: Illustrates a student interviewing twenty hostel residents about laundry before building, and finding cost matters far more than an app.
